story_html:
No fresh weekend catalyst — Friday’s story just kept running. A search for weekend developments (geopolitics, futures, policy announcements) turned up nothing dated Saturday or Sunday that changed the picture; the Fed’s pre-meeting quiet period (Oct 17–29, Chicago Fed calendar) started Saturday, so no officials have spoken since Chair Warsh’s Thursday-night remarks in Bangkok. CNN’s Friday close led with “Nasdaq sinks more than 2% as investors raise questions about AI debt,” reporting the Nasdaq Composite’s worst week since June; Reuters tied the session to a hotter-than-expected inflation print feeding rate-hike bets, and quoted D.A. Davidson’s Gil Luria on whether CoreWeave “can earn enough to repay its borrowing.” CNBC had reported Wednesday that CoreWeave’s bonds were trading near 15% yields on the same AI-borrowing worry; Reuters, citing LSEG, put CoreWeave’s five-year credit-default swaps (insurance against a default) above 1,000bp for the first time, and Oracle’s five-year swaps at a record 288bp, up from 260bp a week earlier.

What the data shows: the selloff widened, not just in one or two names. The S&P 500 fell 1.09% Friday to 7,659.44, 2.04% off its Oct 6 record; the Nasdaq fell 2.14%; the Russell 2000 fell 1.66%. 51 S&P names and sector funds qualified for this system’s movers screen, and the move was lopsided: every one of the dozen-plus biggest decliners sat in the same complex — chipmakers, storage, optical networking, and high-beta software (Movers, below) — while the gainers were almost entirely energy and defense names. The chip fund SMH fell 3.41%, a ninth straight daily decline, down 16.46% from its Jun 22 six-month high per this system’s own tracking. Bonds rallied into the risk-off tape: the 10-year fell 1bp to 5.09% and the 2-year fell 3bp to 4.74%, a mild bull steepener (2s10s widened 2bp to 35bp) — the mirror image of Thursday’s bull flattener. The 10-year has now sat at or above 5.09% since Sep 23; before this run, it was last there in July 2007 (Today in history, below).

Oil jumped and no outlet this system found explained why. WTI rose 3.51% to $101.41, its biggest one-day move since Oct 8, while energy stocks (XLE) still gained 2.52% — unlike Thursday, when oil rose and energy stocks fell for reasons no outlet explained, Friday’s energy-sector move and the oil move agree. Why this matters: a sustained move above $100 WTI shows up at the pump before it shows up anywhere else in a client’s budget, and this system flags it as a watch item, not a conclusion, until a named source explains the move.

The press framing, read plainly. CNN’s and Reuters’ own framing — AI-infrastructure borrowing costs are rising and investors are starting to ask whether the revenue is there to cover them — is their reading, not a conclusion this system can reach from price data alone. What the state file can say: credit spreads for junk-rated borrowers in aggregate (HY OAS) have stayed above both Oct 1’s level and this run’s confirm line for CL-0046 without snapping back, and two single-name credit-default-swap spreads widened further. That is consistent with the press framing; it is not, by itself, proof of it.
dashboard_interp_html:
A small bull steepener, the mirror of Thursday. The 10-year fell 1bp to 5.09% (z +1.54) and the 2-year fell 3bp to 4.74% (z +1.62); the 3-month bill fell 2bp to 4.26% (z +2.11, the dashboard’s second-largest flag after credit). Because the short end fell slightly more than the long end, the curve steepened a touch: 2s10s widened 2bp to 35bp (not flagged). The 30-year was flat at 5.43% (z +1.29, not flagged). Short-term yields falling with long-term yields roughly flat or slightly higher in relative terms is a small bull steepener (Unit 1) — consistent with a market pricing in a little less near-term Fed tightness, not a change in the long-run growth/inflation outlook.

High against the last 30 years, closer to the middle against the full record. The 10-year sits at the 84th percentile of the last 30 years but the 47th since 1962 — a 37-point gap, because the full 64-year record still carries the Volcker-era 1970s/80s double-digit yields that the last 30 years don’t. The 2-year sits at the 82nd percentile over 30 years and the 52nd since 1976. The 3-month bill sits at the 71st over 30 years and the 52nd since 1981. Every maturity reads “unusual lately” against the recent past and roughly average against the long run.

Credit eased slightly on the rally day but stayed wide. HY OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies, still dated 10-15, Thursday) fell 2bp to 3.23% (z +3.36, today’s largest flag by a wide margin), giving back a fifth of Wednesday’s 9bp widening but staying above Oct 1’s 3.24% practically (within a basis point) and above the 3.16% line CL-0046 needs held. IG OAS (the investment-grade version, also dated 10-15) was flat at 0.84% (z +1.88). Both sit in the upper-middle of their own short (~3-year) record here, not extreme on it (§4F). Friday’s own print for both arrives Tuesday.

The dollar (DXY) fell 0.16% to 101.84 (z +1.49, just short of this system’s ±1.5 flag line) — 80th percentile over 30 years, 71st since 1971. SOFR (the overnight bank funding rate) held at 3.88% (z +2.11), in the narrow 3.85%–3.90% band it has kept since September’s hike. This week’s Fed balance-sheet report (H.4.1, still dated 10-14) is unchanged from Friday’s brief at $6.756 trillion, and the Treasury’s cash account (TGA) unchanged at $883.4 billion; both carry forward to Thursday’s next release. ON RRP (money funds’ overnight parking spot at the Fed) swung to $0.1 billion from Thursday’s $1.2 billion — a routine daily swing in a series this system still labels thin history, not a liquidity signal.

Why this matters: mortgage rates track the 10-year, which is flat to slightly lower over the past few sessions, so no fresh relief or pain there this week. Savers in short-term instruments (CDs, money funds, the 3-month bill) keep earning close to 4.3%. For bond-fund holders, the number to keep watching is still credit: junk-bond spreads eased a touch Thursday but stayed close to this run’s own high, above the 3.16% line CL-0046 needs held, and that claim is the live test of whether it holds through Friday.
history_html:
The level, and the run. The 10-year Treasury yield, now 5.09%, has sat at or above that level since Sep 23. Before this run, it was last there in July 2007. Against the last 30 years that’s high (84th percentile); against the full 64-year record it’s about average (47th) — a 37-point gap, since the longer record still carries the Volcker-era 1970s/80s that the last 30 years don’t.

July 2007, then vs. now. The 10-year and real yields line up closely (5.11% then, 5.09% now), with similar breakevens and term premium by this system’s check. The front end doesn’t: the Fed’s rate was 5.25% then against SOFR’s 3.88% now, so the 3-month-to-10-year spread is +83bp today versus +14bp then. The S&P 500 was at a record that day; today it’s 2.04% below one. Even the 30-year mortgage lines up: 6.73% then, 7.40% now.

The speed, not just the level. The 2-year is up 127bp this year, the 9th-largest rise through this date in 50 years. Over the trailing 12 months it’s up 133bp; a rise this big has started 8 times since 1977 — a small sample. From those starts, stocks were lower a year later in 3 of 8 (vs. 24.4% for any 12-month stretch since 1962), and a recession began within two years in 2 of 8 (vs. 27.4% normally).

Why this matters: long-term rates are back to mid-2007 levels, part of why mortgage math feels similarly tough — but the Fed had far more room to cut then, and stocks weren’t 2% off a record the way they are now. A small sample (8 cases): stocks were lower a year later about 3 times in 8 after a rate rise this fast, vs. roughly 1 in 4 normally — worth watching, not a forecast.

concept_unit: Unit 6 — Positioning & sentiment vs. fundamentals, segment 3
concept_title: Priced in, or still getting worse?
concept_html: Segments 1 and 2 built the breadth toolkit: index vs. average, then rotation vs. retreat. This segment asks the harder question behind both. “Priced in” means the bad news is already reflected in the price, so the next incremental data point shouldn’t move it much. “Still worsening” means the underlying driver is still moving, so the price should keep adjusting. The test isn’t how the stock feels — it’s whether the thing actually driving it keeps changing. Here, Oracle’s five-year credit-default swaps widened to a fresh record Thursday (288bp, per Reuters), up from 260bp a week earlier; CoreWeave’s climbed above 1,000bp, a level Reuters said this system hasn’t seen reported before. If those swaps had widened once and then held flat, that would look like a one-time repricing settling into “priced in.” A cost of credit still rising week over week, alongside SMH’s ninth straight down session, is the “still worsening” pattern, not the “already priced in” one. That is exactly why CL-0042 and CL-0046 are built as live tests rather than one-time calls: a pattern that is still unfolding needs to be checked again, not just believed once.
client_translation: When something keeps falling for days in a row, the question that actually matters isn't whether it feels overdone — it's whether the cost of borrowing for those companies is still climbing or has leveled off, and right now it's still climbing.
client_lens_html:
“Did you see what happened to CoreWeave/Oracle?” Both companies’ cost of insuring their own debt against default hit fresh records last week (CoreWeave’s above 1,000bp, Oracle’s at 288bp, both per Reuters) — the market pricing in more risk of a problem, not a problem that has already happened. CoreWeave’s CEO told CNN its contracted backlog covers its debt; that is the company’s own statement, not verified here. This system makes no call on any specific position (§8); the flag below routes it to the right process.

“Is this an AI bubble popping, or just a rough patch?” The honest answer: this system can’t tell from nine sessions of SMH data. What it can say is that the move is broad (a dozen-plus chip, storage, and software names, not one), and that credit — the better tie-breaker per Unit 3 — is still pricing more risk, not less. CL-0042 and CL-0046 are the live tests of whether that continues through next week.

“Why did gas prices jump?” WTI rose 3.51% Friday to $101.41. No named source this system found explained the specific move; it’s a watch item for the pump, not yet a confirmed cause-and-effect story.
